rationale: The book's identification of 'the heart of the earth' as Jerusalem is the only reading among the actual alternatives that rests on Scripture's own usage of the phrase-family. No biblical text ever calls a grave or Hades 'the heart of the earth,' whereas Ezekiel 5:5 explicitly locates Jerusalem 'in the midst of the nations' and Ezekiel 38:12 uses tabbur ha'aretz ('navel of the land,' the same word as Judges 9:37) of the regathered people's center. The decisive internal control is the mirrored phrase in Jonah's own prayer: Jonah says he was cast 'into the heart of the seas' (bilvav yammim, Jonah 2:3, flattened to 'midst' in the KJV). Since the sea is a scripturally defined symbol for peoples and nations (Rev 17:15, and accepted upstream via the Ship premise where the sea bears political vessels), 'heart of the seas' means the center of the gentile world — and the mirrored 'heart of the earth/land' means the center of the covenant land, the city God set in the midst of the nations. The counter-reading (tomb/Sheol) must import its referent from theological association (Acts 2:27; Eph 4:9 — different phrases entirely) rather than from any text using the actual expression, and it generates the notorious three-days-and-three-nights counting problem that the book's reading dissolves: seized into Jerusalem's custody on the night of betrayal, out on the third day (Luke 24:21). The book also answers the strongest counter directly: Jonah in the fish is alive and praying, 'as good as dead' behind the earth's bars, so the Sheol language of Jonah 2 describes the condition inside the swallowing power's custody, which the Jerusalem reading contains (death and burial occur within the interval) rather than excludes. The counter explains no material detail the book cannot; the book explains the lexical evidence, the mirrored Hebrew phrase, the extrabiblical recognition (Philo, Sibylline Oracles), and the chronology that the tomb reading cannot.
book_core_identification: 'The heart of the earth' in Matthew 12:40 refers to Jerusalem — the city God set in the midst of the nations, the navel and heart of the land (Ezek 5:5; 38:12) — so that the three days and three nights measure the Son of Man's time under Jerusalem's power, from His seizure into the city's custody to His coming out on the third day.
book_secondary_elaborations: The three-day count begins at the arrest outside the gates on the night of betrayal rather than at burial, dissolving the Friday-to-Sunday counting problem (Luke 24:13, 21)
The full scene-by-scene Jonah–Passion typology (ship = Judean polity, storm = rulers' fear of Rome, great fish = Caesar/Rome as the devouring ruler, casting = surrender of one man for the nation)

Extrabiblical corroboration: Philo calling Jerusalem the 'heart of the whole earth,' the Sibylline Oracles' 'navel and heart of the earth,' and Greek Ezekiel manuscripts substituting 'heart' for 'navel'
The Hebrew wordplay analysis (bilvav yammim, tabbur ha'aretz) and the claim that KJV 'midst' flattens both key phrases
The extension of the sign to the post-resurrection gentile mission and Israel's jealousy (Jonah 3–4 as prophecy of Acts 13 and Romans 11)
strongest_counter_interpretation: 'The heart of the earth' means the grave/tomb — and in fuller traditional form, the realm of the dead (Sheol/Hades) — during the interval between Jesus' death and resurrection. The typological logic is containment in death: as Jonah was enclosed in the fish's belly and cried 'out of the belly of Sheol' (Jonah 2:2), so Jesus was enclosed in death, buried in the earth (Matt 27:57-60), his soul not abandoned to Hades (Ps 16:10; Acts 2:24-31), having 'descended into the lower parts of the earth' (Eph 4:9), before rising the third day (1 Cor 15:3-4).
counter_core_identification: The phrase designates Jesus' entombment/sojourn in the realm of the dead — the grave or Sheol/Hades — not any geographic location on the earth's surface.
material_core_denial: Both identifications cannot be true as the referent of the measured interval: if 'heart of the earth' is the tomb/Sheol, the three days and nights run from burial to resurrection and cannot include the arrest, trials, and crucifixion; if it is Jerusalem, the interval runs from the city's seizure of Jesus and necessarily includes those events. The two readings assign the phrase different referents and different starting points, and the tomb reading entails that the count begins only at burial — which the Jerusalem reading denies.
counter_case: Jonah explicitly names his location 'the belly of Sheol' (Jonah 2:2), suggesting the antitype is the realm of the dead, not a city

The immediate parallel structure of Matt 12:40 pairs 'the whale's belly' with 'the heart of the earth' as matching enclosures, and the fish's belly is a death-image (Jonah 2:6: 'the earth with her bars was about me')
Acts 2:24-31 applies Psalm 16:10 to Christ's soul in Hades and flesh not seeing corruption, tying the interval to death and burial
Eph 4:9 ('descended into the lower parts of the earth') and 1 Pet 3:18-19 anchor a broad traditional descent-to-the-dead reading
1 Cor 15:3-4 counts 'the third day' from death and burial, and Matt 27:57-60 supplies the tomb as an obvious concrete referent
This is the overwhelming consensus reading across all three independent common-interpretation responses
book_explanatory_advantages: Scripture itself supplies the identification: Ezek 5:5 names Jerusalem as set 'in the midst of the nations,' and Ezek 38:12 uses tabbur ha'aretz ('navel of the land'), the exact figure the entry claims; no verse anywhere calls a grave 'the heart of the earth'

The mirrored Hebrew phrase in Jonah 2:3 — bilvav yammim, 'in the heart of the seas' — reads by Scripture's own symbol dictionary (sea = peoples/nations, Rev 17:15) as the center of the gentile world, making 'heart of the earth/land' the center of the covenant land by exact parallel; the sign's two phrases decode each other
It dissolves the three-days-and-three-nights chronology problem without calendar gymnastics: seized into Jerusalem's custody the night of betrayal, out on the third day (Luke 24:21)

It accounts for the Sheol language rather than ignoring it: Jonah is alive and praying inside the fish, 'as good as dead,' just as Jesus' death and burial fall within — not instead of — the Jerusalem-custody interval

It integrates the whole Jonah narrative as Luke frames it ('Jonah was a sign unto the Ninevites,' Luke 11:30): the ship (Judean polity, per the accepted Ship premise), the storm, the interrogation, the casting, the fish (Rome/Caesar as devouring ruler, per Jer 51:34, 44; Ezek 29:3; 32:2), and the mission to the nations
Contemporary usage corroborates: Philo and the Sibylline Oracles independently call Jerusalem the heart/navel of the earth, showing Jesus' hearers could recognize the referent
counter_explanatory_advantages: It preserves the most immediate surface parallel of Matt 12:40: belly-as-enclosure matched to earth-as-enclosure, both places of death
It coheres directly with Jonah's own 'belly of Sheol' cry and with Acts 2:27's Hades language applied to Christ
It aligns with 1 Cor 15:4's 'buried... raised the third day' sequence and requires no relocation of the count's starting point
It carries near-universal traditional and scholarly support
decisive_sources: Ezekiel 5:5 ('This is Jerusalem: I have set it in the midst of the nations')
Ezekiel 38:12 with Judges 9:37 (tabbur ha'aretz, 'navel of the land')
Jonah 2:3 Hebrew bilvav yammim ('in the heart of the seas'), the mirrored phrase to Matt 12:40
Revelation 17:15 (waters = peoples, multitudes, nations) supplying the symbol-dictionary for the mirror
Luke 24:13, 21 ('today is the third day since these things were done') fixing the count's endpoint
Prior accepted Ship finding (FULL): the ship as governed political body, grounding the Jonah 1 / John 11:48-50 parallel (Caiaphas's bargain)
Jeremiah 51:34, 44; Ezekiel 29:3; 32:2 (devouring ruler swallowing and forced to give back), grounding the great fish as Rome/Caesar rather than the grave itself
Philo and Sibylline Oracles calling Jerusalem the heart/navel of the earth (corroborative, not probative)
unresolved_objections: Luke 24:21's 'third day since these things were done' most naturally counts from the crucifixion complex rather than the arrest specifically; the precise start-point of the book's count (arrest night vs. condemnation) remains an argued elaboration, though the full calendar case is deferred to another work
Jesus was crucified and buried outside the city wall; the book's claim that custody by Jerusalem's polity keeps Him 'in' the heart of the earth throughout is a defensible but inferential step

The traditional descent texts (Eph 4:9; Acts 2:27; 1 Pet 3:18-19) retain independent force for a Sheol dimension of the interval; the book absorbs rather than refutes them, and a reader could still hold a layered reading in which Sheol imagery is secondary within the Jerusalem referent
The Philo/Sibylline witnesses are extrabiblical and, as the book concedes, only corroborative
